reasoning_traces.think:
The core innovation lies in the O(log n) combinatorial design that minimizes the number of distinct assortments needed for accurate choice estimation while maintaining theoretical optimality. This is achieved by leveraging the boost factor BF(i,S) = P(i,S)/P(i,[n]), which quantifies how much more likely an item is to be chosen under a specific assortment versus baseline. For nest identification, this ratio allows distinguishing between items in the same nest (identical boost) and those in different nests (distinct boosts). The algorithmic approach uses a deduction process based on comparing boost factors across assortments to build a transitive adjacency matrix, effectively reconstructing the underlying nest structure. In practice, this translates into efficient experimental protocols where only a logarithmic number of carefully selected assortments suffice to recover complex choice behaviors. The method's strength stems from its ability to handle misspecified models gracefully, especially when dealing with synthetic benchmarks like Berbeglia et al.'s framework, where even imperfect models can be evaluated robustly. Furthermore, the deployment at Dream11 validates scalability and effectiveness in real-world settings involving millions of users and diverse contest types.
